function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below are the three files you’ll need to add to the **nodejs‑welcome** repository, followed by a quick “cheat‑sheet” of the Git commands that will get everything committed and pushed.

---

## 1️⃣ Dockerfile (root of the repo)

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – lightweight Node runtime
FROM node:14-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy dependency descriptors first so Docker can cache the install step
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command – runs the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:14-alpine` is small, fast, and stable for most Node apps.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean, reproducible install.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` matches the typical Express default.  
> * `CMD ["npm", "start"]` lets you keep the same start script you use locally.

---

## 2️⃣ Kubernetes YAML (create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml`)

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: myrepo/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry/repo
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # external port
    targetPort: 3000  # container port
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys two replicas of your app.  
> * Exposes them via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80, forwarding to the container’s port 3000.  
> * Replace `myrepo/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual image name/tag you’ll push to Docker Hub (or another registry).

---

## 3️⃣ GitHub Actions Workflow (create a file called `.github/workflows/ci.yml`)

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI/CD

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Docker Buildx (multi‑platform builder)
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

      # Log in to Docker Hub (you’ll need to set these secrets in the repo settings)
      - name: Login to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the image and push it to Docker Hub
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: myrepo/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your image name/tag
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggered on every push to `main`.  
> * Builds the Docker image from the Dockerfile in the repo root.  
> * Pushes the image to Docker Hub (or any registry you configure).  
> * Requires two repository secrets: `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`.

---

## 4️⃣ Git Commands (run from the repo root)

```bash
# 1️⃣ Stage the new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# 2️⃣ Commit with a meaningful message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"

# 3️⃣ Push to the remote (assumes you’re on the main branch)
git push origin main
```

> **Tip:** If you haven’t already, make sure the `k8s` and `.github/workflows` directories exist before running `git add`.  
> If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

### Quick sanity check

| File | Path | Purpose |
|------|------|---------|
| Dockerfile | `/Dockerfile` | Container image definition |
| Deployment & Service | `/k8s/deployment.yaml` | Kubernetes deployment + service |
| CI workflow | `/.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions pipeline |

Once you push, GitHub Actions will automatically build and push your Docker image whenever you push to `main`. The Kubernetes YAML can then be applied to any cluster with `kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml`.

Happy coding! 🚀
